items.question: Which drug is used in hyperthyroidism to block hormone synthesis?
items.explanation: Carbimazole (and methimazole) inhibit thyroid peroxidase, blocking thyroid hormone synthesis.

items.question: Methotrexate toxicity is rescued by?
items.explanation: Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescues normal cells. Mesna prevents cyclophosphamide cystitis; dexrazoxane protects from anthracyclines.

items.question: HLA-B*1502 testing before which drug reduces Stevens-Johnson risk?
items.explanation: HLA-B*1502 (common in Asians) predicts carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN; testing is advised before starting.

items.question: Antidote for benzodiazepine overdose is?
items.explanation: Flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine receptor antagonist; use cautiously as it may precipitate seizures.

items.question: William Withering is known for introducing which drug?
items.explanation: William Withering described the use of digitalis (foxglove) for dropsy (heart failure) in 1785.

*PharmaCraft Daily - 22 Oct 2026*

🎓 *MBBS* (Endocrine)
Q: Which drug is used in hyperthyroidism to block hormone synthesis?
Ans: Carbimazole
Why: Carbimazole (and methimazole) inhibit thyroid peroxidase, blocking thyroid hormone synthesis.

🩺 *NEET PG* (Anticancer)
Q: Methotrexate toxicity is rescued by?
Ans: Folinic acid
Why: Leucovorin (folinic acid) rescues normal cells. Mesna prevents cyclophosphamide cystitis; dexrazoxane protects from anthracyclines.

🏥 *INI-CET* (Pharmacogenomics)
Q: HLA-B*1502 testing before which drug reduces Stevens-Johnson risk?
Ans: Carbamazepine
Why: HLA-B*1502 (common in Asians) predicts carbamazepine-induced SJS/TEN; testing is advised before starting.

🌍 *FMGE* (Toxicology)
Q: Antidote for benzodiazepine overdose is?
Ans: Flumazenil
Why: Flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine receptor antagonist; use cautiously as it may precipitate seizures.

🔬 *MD Pharmacology* (History of Pharmacology)
Q: William Withering is known for introducing which drug?
Ans: Digitalis
Why: William Withering described the use of digitalis (foxglove) for dropsy (heart failure) in 1785.
